title: Data Manipulation & Querying (DML & DQL)
relevance: SDE interviews and OAs heavily grill SQL SELECT complexity—logical execution order, joins, aggregations, and NULL semantics—because day-to-day backend work depends on writing correct queries.

phases.goal: Establish what DML vs DQL do and the basic surface of SELECT, WHERE, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE.

must_hit.point: DML modifies data inside the structure (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE); DQL retrieves it (SELECT).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate cleanly separates mutating statements from SELECT as the retrieve/query side.

must_hit.point: WHERE is a row-level sieve using comparison operators, inclusive BETWEEN, IN, LIKE patterns, and IS NULL / IS NOT NULL—not = NULL.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They list common operators and stress IS NULL for unknown values rather than equality to NULL.

must_hit.point: INSERT can be single-row, multi-row, INSERT…SELECT, or DEFAULT VALUES; omitted columns get their DEFAULT or NULL.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They describe specifying columns/VALUES and what happens when a column is left out.

must_hit.point: DELETE removes entire rows; clearing one column requires UPDATE SET column = NULL, not DELETE of a column.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They distinguish row removal from nulling a field via UPDATE.

probes: What is the difference between DML and DQL, and what does a basic SELECT with WHERE look like?
How do INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE differ in what they change?

hints.1: Think about whether the statement changes stored rows or only reads them.
hints.2: Map INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE to mutation and SELECT to retrieval; WHERE decides which rows participate.
hints.3: DML = insert/update/delete data; DQL = SELECT; WHERE filters rows with operators like =, BETWEEN, IN, LIKE, IS NULL.

phases.goal: Establish logical clause execution order, join semantics, and how GROUP BY/HAVING and aggregates actually run.

must_hit.point: Logical execution order is FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT/OFFSET—not the typed syntax order.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They recite that pipeline and contrast it with how you write the query.

must_hit.point: A SELECT alias cannot be used in WHERE (or typically GROUP BY) because WHERE runs before SELECT creates the alias; repeat the expression in WHERE.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They explain why WHERE total_comp > 100000 fails when total_comp is only defined in SELECT.

must_hit.point: INNER JOIN keeps matches only; LEFT/RIGHT keep one side with NULLs on miss; FULL OUTER keeps both sides; CROSS JOIN is the Cartesian product; SELF JOIN joins a table to itself.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They can sketch each join outcome on employees/departments and mention self-join for manager hierarchies.

must_hit.point: WHERE filters raw rows before grouping; HAVING filters aggregated buckets after GROUP BY—so WHERE AVG(...) is invalid at that stage.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They place WHERE before buckets and HAVING after aggregates, with a correct dept average example shape.

must_hit.point: COUNT(*) counts all rows; COUNT(column) counts only non-NULL values in that column.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They note a NULL salary is included by COUNT(*) but skipped by COUNT(salary).

must_hit.point: LATERAL (Postgres) lets a FROM subquery reference prior tables so each outer row can drive a correlated subquery (e.g. top earners per department with ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 3).
must_hit.evidence_hint: They say LATERAL re-runs the subquery per outer row, breaking the usual FROM-subquery reference rule.

probes: Walk me through the logical execution order of a SELECT with WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, and ORDER BY.
What is the difference between INNER, LEFT, and CROSS JOIN, and when would you use HAVING instead of WHERE?

hints.1: Ignore how you type the query; think about what the engine must compute first.
hints.2: Build the row set (FROM/JOIN), filter rows (WHERE), bucket (GROUP BY), filter buckets (HAVING), then project/sort/limit.
hints.3: Order is FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT/OFFSET; aliases from SELECT are not visible in WHERE.

phases.goal: Contrast UPSERT approaches, MERGE vs ON CONFLICT, and UNION vs UNION ALL on correctness and cost.

must_hit.point: INSERT…ON CONFLICT is one atomic UPSERT; SELECT-then-INSERT/UPDATE from app code races if another process inserts between the check and write.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They reject check-then-write and cite ON CONFLICT / EXCLUDED as thread-safe for unique conflicts.

must_hit.point: MERGE suits complex sync between tables (WHEN MATCHED / NOT MATCHED insert/update/delete); ON CONFLICT only reacts to unique-constraint violations on insert.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They say MERGE can sync on join match/non-match; ON CONFLICT is narrower insert conflict handling.

must_hit.point: UNION removes duplicates and forces a sort/dedup over the combined set; UNION ALL keeps duplicates and avoids that cost when sets are disjoint or duplicates are fine.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They prefer UNION ALL for performance when dedup is unnecessary.

must_hit.point: Naming columns explicitly instead of SELECT * cuts network traffic and memory versus shipping every column.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They tie explicit projection to less data transferred and used.

probes: When would you use INSERT…ON CONFLICT versus MERGE, and why prefer UNION ALL over UNION?
Why is SELECT-then-INSERT a bad UPSERT pattern under concurrency?

hints.1: Separate 'handle one unique conflict on insert' from 'reconcile two whole tables'.
hints.2: Atomic conflict handling vs join-based MATCHED/NOT MATCHED; set ops differ on whether dedup is required.
hints.3: ON CONFLICT = atomic UPSERT on unique violation; MERGE = richer sync; UNION ALL skips UNION's dedup sort when duplicates don't matter.

phases.goal: Apply joins, NULL helpers, CASE, and safe DML patterns to typical interview query scenarios.

must_hit.point: LEFT JOIN is the tool for finding missing links (e.g. employees with no matching department, dept_name NULL).
must_hit.evidence_hint: They write or describe LEFT JOIN from employees to departments and filter on NULL right-side keys.

must_hit.point: COALESCE picks the first non-NULL argument; NULLIF(a,b) returns NULL when equal—used as NULLIF(cost, 0) so division becomes NULL instead of dividing by zero.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They give COALESCE for contact fallback and NULLIF to neutralize a zero divisor.

must_hit.point: CASE (simple or searched) returns a value from conditions; SUM(CASE WHEN…) enables conditional aggregation to pivot row categories into columns.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They show banding salaries with CASE or counting high vs other earners via SUM(CASE WHEN…).

must_hit.point: For critical UPDATE/DELETE, write the WHERE first or run inside a transaction with ROLLBACK ready—omitting WHERE updates or deletes every row.
must_hit.evidence_hint: They warn that UPDATE without WHERE can set every salary and stress transactional safety.

probes: How would you find all employees who have no department assigned?
How do you safely raise salaries for one department, and how would you avoid division-by-zero in a margin query?

hints.1: Think about preserving every employee even when the department lookup fails.
hints.2: Outer join for missing departments; COALESCE/NULLIF for NULLs; always constrain mutating DML.
hints.3: LEFT JOIN employees to departments and filter NULL dept; COALESCE/NULLIF for defaults and zero divisors; never UPDATE/DELETE without WHERE unless intentional.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: ON CONFLICT does UPSERT in one atomic step using EXCLUDED for the proposed row; app-level SELECT then INSERT/UPDATE can race if another process inserts in between.

ON CONFLICT handles unique violations during insert; MERGE joins target and source and can INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on MATCHED vs NOT MATCHED for full table synchronization (supported from PostgreSQL 15).
UNION appends and removes duplicates (sort/dedup cost); UNION ALL keeps duplicates and is preferred when sets are already disjoint or duplicates do not matter.
WHERE filters raw rows before GROUP BY; HAVING filters aggregate buckets after grouping—aggregate predicates belong in HAVING, not WHERE.
Explicit column lists reduce network traffic and memory versus SELECT *, which pulls every column.

gotchas.trap: Referencing a SELECT alias in WHERE or GROUP BY (e.g. WHERE total_comp > 100000 when total_comp is defined only in SELECT).
gotchas.correction: Logical order evaluates WHERE before SELECT; repeat the expression in WHERE instead of the alias.

gotchas.trap: Using WHERE manager_id = NULL (or any = NULL comparison).
gotchas.correction: NULL means unknown; equality to NULL is unknown/never true in WHERE—use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL.

gotchas.trap: NOT IN with a subquery (or list) that contains NULL, e.g. NOT IN (1, 2, NULL).
gotchas.correction: The predicate becomes unknown for every row and returns zero results; filter NULLs out of the subquery when using NOT IN.

gotchas.trap: UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE clause.
gotchas.correction: Every row is mutated or removed with no undo outside a transaction—write WHERE first or wrap in a transaction ready to ROLLBACK.

gotchas.trap: SELECT * FROM A, B with no join predicate.
gotchas.correction: That is an implicit CROSS JOIN/Cartesian product that can explode into huge result sets; use explicit JOIN … ON ….

gotchas.trap: Assuming COUNT(*) and COUNT(column) are the same.
gotchas.correction: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) skips NULLs in that column.

gotchas.trap: Putting aggregate conditions in WHERE, e.g. WHERE AVG(salary) > 70000.
gotchas.correction: Aggregates are not available until after grouping; filter buckets with HAVING after GROUP BY.
